newsitem.title: FINLAND: FOCUS-MEDIA MERGERS TURN UP HEAT IN NORDIC MARKETS.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-MEDIA MERGERS TURN UP HEAT IN NORDIC MARKETS.

text.p: A battle for market share in Nordic media took a new turn on Tuesday as Finnish media group Aamulehti, facing mounting competition from local rival Sanoma Oy, said it would merge with domestic broadcaster MTV Oy.
"By combining two ... strong communications experts, we create a significant media group also on a European scale," Aamulehti Oy CEO Matti Packalen said in a statement.

Commentators saw the deal -- which to some extent merely confirmed a process already underway dividing ownership of the main commercial channels into two camps -- as also a breakthrough for foreign interests in Finnish television.

Aamulehti said the new bourse-listed company, to be created in 1998, would have net annual sales around 2.5 billion markka and 2,600 full-time employees -- more than the 1.8 billion markka net sales and 1,740 staff at Sanoma in 1996.

Talks started in early spring but the news came just days after Sanoma, Aamulehti's chief rival and publisher of leading national daily Helsingin Sanomat, said it planned a major expansion into electronic and print business news.
That would be a direct competitor to Aamulehti's highly profitable Kauppalehti business daily, which has to date dominated the business news market in print.
Helena Tapper, senior lecturer at Helsinki University's Department of Communications, said the deal could be viewed as a key battle in the war between Sweden's Marieberg and Finnish-owned Sanoma Oy.

Last year Sanoma beat Aamulehti, whose biggest owner is Marieberg, to clinch the concession for a new commercial television station, Nelonen, prompting Aamulehti to boost ties with MTV -- strong in the Finnish television advertising market.
Aamulehti's shares surged in Helsinki in response to the deal, scaling a new year high of 196.00 markka and trading up 38.50 markka or 25 percent at 193.00 in late dealings.

"I guess the market could expect some kind of consolidation whereby Marieberg could acquire Aamulehti," said Uls Hellzen, analyst at Swedbank in Stockholm. "It would be a good guess but it's a tough one to crack, for control and nationality reasons."

Marieberg said later on Tuesday it had increased its holding in Aamulehti to over 28 percent of shares and votes, and would retain about 20 percent overall in the new group. Its stock was marked up 3.5 crowns at 193.00 crowns.

For Marieberg, controlled by Sweden's Bonnier family with over 75 percent of votes, Tapper said the deal was a "grand entree". Through Aamulehti alone, foreigners in Finnish media had been confined to print and radio.
Aamulehti said the new company would have a strong market share in the print, electronic and audiovisual sectors and be a front-runner in the area of new media and digital technology.

Aamulehti also publishes a leading tabloid newspaper, Iltalehti; it is already active in radio, and several of its publications have moved into electronic real-time publishing, including on the Internet.
The merging companies said they had both had strong earnings in recent years and the merger would guarantee strength in the balance sheet and profitability from the start.
Pending approval by the authorities for the deal, Aamulehti shares would be converted into the new company's shares at one-to-one with shares in MTV converted at one to 137.5.
After the Aamulehti statement and separately, Finland's main news stand retailer Rautakirja said Sanoma had boosted its share in it to over 20 percent.
